subject: zoology
question_text: What do you call the first and second pairs of cephalic appendages of a scorpion?

verification.note: Sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack zoology section (book p.54, VSAQ 100). Zoology holds only ONE source book — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only, and no zoology board paper is in the corpus — so the two-book union check and the back-test are both structurally impossible for this card; 'not checked' does NOT mean 'checked and clean'. The mark split is a claim until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The first pair
steps.why: The two pairs are named in the order in which they lie from the front of the animal, so counting back from the mouth keeps them in the right order.
common_mistakes: Calling the first pair antennae. Chelicerates have no antennae.
Writing that the chelicerae are the large pincers. The large pincers are the pedipalps.
steps.memory_tip: Small pincers first (chelicerae), big pincers second (pedipalps).
steps.margin_note: Name the pair and add one line on what it does.
lines: The prosoma of a scorpion carries six pairs of
The first pair are the chelicerae.
They are small and pincer-like, and they tear
the food before it is taken in.

steps.label: The second pair
steps.why: The pedipalps are the pair that reaches the prey first, which is why they are the largest appendages on the body.
common_mistakes: Writing walking legs. The walking legs are the third to the sixth pairs.
Naming only one of the two pairs. Both are asked for.
steps.memory_tip: Six pairs on the prosoma: chelicerae, pedipalps, then four pairs of legs.
steps.margin_note: Two names is the whole answer. Two short lines each is enough.
lines: The second pair are the pedipalps.
They are large pincers used to catch and hold
The remaining four pairs are the walking legs.

insider_note: Two names carry the two marks; the sentence on what each pair does is what saves you if one name is misspelt.
